scenes.narration: Your classmate Riya looks uneasy. An older family friend insists on hugs every time he visits, even after she pulls away. 'Maybe I'm overreacting?' she asks you.

choices.text: You're not overreacting. Your body, your rules. You can say no to ANY touch, even from someone familiar.
choices.feedback: Right. Consent applies to everyone, including family friends. Boundaries are a right, not rudeness, and the POCSO Act protects everyone under 18 from unwanted contact, whoever it comes from.

choices.text: He's a family friend. She should just put up with it.
choices.feedback: Familiarity never cancels consent. Much of the harm children face comes from people they already know, which is exactly why the law says no one, however close, may cross a child's boundaries.

choices.text: Tell her to quietly avoid him.
choices.feedback: Avoiding can be a short-term shield, but boundaries deserve words too. Riya can say no clearly and tell a parent or trusted adult how the behaviour makes her feel. She has every right to.

scenes.narration: Later, your friend Arjun (14) shows you his chats. An online 'friend' he has never met, who claims to be 15, showers him with compliments, sends free game credits, and says: 'Don't tell your parents about us. They wouldn't understand our friendship.' What do you see?

choices.text: Flattery, gifts, and 'keep us secret' from someone he's never met. Those are grooming red flags.
choices.feedback: Sharp eyes. People who target children online often build trust with gifts and compliments, then isolate the child with secrecy. Spotting the pattern early is the best protection there is.

choices.text: Sounds like a really generous friend.
choices.feedback: Real friends don't demand secrecy from your family. Gifts plus flattery plus secrecy from a stranger is a manipulation pattern called grooming, and the law treats luring a child this way as a serious offence.

scenes.narration: A week later, the 'friend' pushes harder: 'Send me a private photo. Everyone does it. If you're really my friend, prove it.' Arjun feels trapped. What should he do?

choices.text: Refuse, stop replying, keep the chats as proof, and tell a trusted adult right away.
choices.feedback: Exactly. Arjun did nothing wrong by chatting; the wrong is entirely the other person's. Saving the messages helps adults act. Asking anyone under 18 for such photos is a crime under POCSO, full stop.

choices.text: Send one photo so he doesn't lose the friendship.
choices.feedback: A 'friendship' that demands photos as proof is a trap, not a friendship. Once sent, a photo can never be taken back. The safe move is to refuse and tell a trusted adult. Arjun will not be blamed for someone else's crime.

choices.text: Just block him and never mention it to anyone.
choices.feedback: Blocking stops the messages, but telling a trusted adult matters too. It protects Arjun AND other kids this person may be targeting. Childline 1098 can also guide the next steps, free of charge, any day, any time.

scenes.narration: You and Arjun talk it through. He asks quietly: 'Is any of this my fault? Is there even a law about things like this?'

choices.text: The POCSO Act protects everyone under 18, online and offline. The fault is one hundred percent the groomer's.
choices.feedback: Correct. The POCSO Act, 2012 covers sexual harassment and exploitation of anyone under 18, including through the internet. A child is never at fault for an adult's crime. That is the whole point of the law.

choices.text: He shouldn't have chatted online at all, so it's partly his fault.
choices.feedback: No. Making friends online is normal; exploiting a child is a crime. The responsibility sits entirely with the person who crossed the line, and the law is explicit about that.

scenes.narration: Arjun tells his older sister everything. Together they block and report the account, and call Childline 1098 to ask what to do next. The counsellor tells him: 'You did the right thing. This was never your fault.' Arjun finally breathes easy, and you realise he came to you first because you knew the signals.

choices.text: Speaking up turned a scary secret into a solved problem.
choices.feedback: That is the whole lesson. Clear boundaries, red-flag radar, and one trusted adult, or a free call to Childline 1098, is the combination that keeps you and your friends safe.

choices.text: Arjun got lucky. Usually telling adults just makes things worse.
choices.feedback: Telling a trusted adult or Childline 1098 is exactly how children get protected. Reporting is designed to help the child, never to punish them. Staying silent is what keeps the problem alive.

quizQuestions.question: What does consent mean?
options: Saying yes because you feel pressured
A free, clear yes, and you can change your mind or say no anytime
Something only adults need to think about
quizQuestions.explanation: Consent is a freely given yes. Pressure, tricks, or fear cancel it, and you always have the right to say no to unwanted touch, whoever is asking.

quizQuestions.question: Which of these is a grooming red flag?
options: An online stranger sending gifts and saying 'keep our chats secret'
A friend sharing a funny video
quizQuestions.explanation: Gifts, heavy flattery, and demands for secrecy from someone you've never met are classic grooming moves, designed to cut you off from the people who protect you.

quizQuestions.question: Who does the POCSO Act protect?
options: Everyone under 18, including from online harassment
quizQuestions.explanation: POCSO protects every person under 18, of every gender, from sexual abuse, harassment, and exploitation, both offline and online.

quizQuestions.question: Someone online pressures you for private photos. What's the best response?
options: Send one to keep the peace
Refuse, save the evidence, and tell a trusted adult or call Childline 1098
Keep arguing with them in the chat
quizQuestions.explanation: Refusing and telling is the safe play. Demanding such photos from a minor is a crime, and the child who reports it is protected by law, never punished.
